01 · Overview

Measuring whether the new app
actually works for real users

UKRSIBBANK launched a redesigned mobile app — UKRSIB Online 2.0. Before scaling it to all users, we needed to understand: can people actually use it? Not just whether it looks good, but whether core banking tasks are findable, understandable, and completable without friction.

We ran a structured moderated usability study with 14–15 participants across two segments, testing 9 key scenarios in Maze. Each scenario had pre-defined hypotheses, entry points, success criteria, and follow-up questions. Results were tracked using Task Success, Time on Task, Error Rate, and User Satisfaction (SUM).

9 tasks
Scenarios tested — from card number copying and transfers to utility payments, currency exchange, and deposit opening
14–15 p.
Participants across 2 segments: users who migrated from the old app and users who only used the old version
4 metrics
Task Success · Time on Task · Error Rate · User Satisfaction (SUM scale 1–5) — tracked per scenario per participant

02 · Research Design

Four steps from hypothesis
to validated insight

Step 01

Research Plan

Defined 4 goals: measure task effectiveness, identify navigation pain points, collect usability metrics, gather hypotheses for quantitative validation.

Step 02

Audience

Segment A: existing users who tried 2.0 and returned to the old app (7–8 people). Segment B: users who only used the old version (7–8 people).

Step 03

Scenarios & Script

9 scenarios ranked simple→complex. Full moderated script: intro, warm-up, banking experience screening, prototype rules, 9 tasks with follow-up questions each.

Step 04

Testing in Maze

45–60 min per session via Zoom. Video recording, notes, Maze metric tracking. Each task had defined entry point, success state, and error classification.

03 · Tested Scenarios

9 real banking tasks,
ranked by complexity

Each scenario was a real-life situation — "your friend wants to send you money for coffee," "an online store needs your IBAN to refund you," "your internet payment failed, change your limit." Ranked from simplest to most complex, so early tasks built confidence before harder ones.

04 · Interview Script

Structured moderation —
same script for all 15 sessions

Every session followed the same structure: intro and consent → 5-min warm-up (where they live, banking experience, what they use the app for) → screening (experience with UKRSIB 2.0, other banks, device type) → prototype rules → 9 tasks with situational prompts → closing (easiest/hardest task, overall navigation rating).

Participants were explicitly told: "Everything you do today is correct — there are no wrong answers." They were asked to think aloud throughout.

Moderated session script · Group B scenario order · Intro → Warm-up → Rules → 9 tasks with follow-ups → Closing

05 · Participants

10 respondents profiled —
real banking behaviour, real friction

Each participant was screened for banking history with UKRSIBBANK, experience with the new app, what operations they perform regularly, and what frustrates them most about banking apps. Two contrasting respondents illustrate the range: P1 (Наталя, 28, teacher from Mukachevo — uses multiple banks, new app installed 2 weeks ago but not yet needed) and P2 (Марина, 36, psychologist — UKRSIBBANK salary card for 7 years, still uses the old app).

06 · Hypotheses

Every scenario started
with a testable hypothesis

Before running sessions, we formulated specific hypotheses for each task — things we expected users to struggle with based on heuristic analysis of the prototype. These became the lens through which we observed each session and coded observations.

Task 02 · Transfer to card

H1: Users won't immediately find the transfer function — it's hidden behind multiple steps (Home → Card → Payments → Transfer).

H2: Users expect to find transfer on the home screen, not via card.

H3: Users can't distinguish "transfer to card" vs "transfer via IBAN" and may confuse them.

Task 03 · Mobile top-up

H1: Users expect to find mobile top-up directly on the home screen — and it works.

H2: Absence of autofill or suggestions when entering a number may cause errors.

H3: No custom amount field may limit flexibility for some users.

Task 04 · Share requisites

H1: Users will look for requisites in "Account Details," not in "Actions."

H2: "Account requisites and QR code" label may be non-obvious for users simply looking for "Requisites."

H3: Users want to share requisites via messenger, email, or copy to clipboard.

Task 06 · Pay utilities

H1: Interface should allow quick selection of the correct utility without additional prompts.

H2: The "add new address" function placement may not be intuitive.

H3: Visual hierarchy of elements may not match user expectations of what's primary vs secondary.

Task 07 · Set limits

H1: Finding the limits settings in the app structure may be difficult.

H2: It may be unclear which types of limits can be changed (total, online, ATM).

H3: The process of changing a limit should look secure and controlled (SMS confirmation).

Task 05 · IBAN transfer

H1: Users may not understand that this is a transfer to another bank's account, not a card — critical for correct flow selection.

H2: Users may not understand what to put in "Payment purpose" — especially when paying for goods.

Hypothesis cards per scenario — used as observation guides during moderated sessions

07 · Results Fixation

Observations coded per task,
per participant

After each session, observations were logged into a structured results matrix — task by task, participant by participant. Comments, hesitations, errors, and notable quotes were recorded. This allowed cross-participant pattern identification and validated (or invalidated) the pre-session hypotheses.

"It was exactly as I expected — one tap."

— Participant on Task 1 (copy card number) · most intuitive task across all sessions

Results fixation · Tasks 1–6 · Comments and observations per participant (P1–P10) · color-coded by success/failure/partial

Task 01 · Copy card number · Finding

Fast execution. Most participants completed in one tap. "It was exactly as I expected." Commission notice was ignored by most — potential risk for paid operations.

Task 02 · Transfer to card · Finding

Entry point confusion. Participants didn't immediately notice the commission. Others preferred the path via Payments over via card. "Better than the old app — IBAN and card are clearly separated."

Task 03 · Mobile top-up · Finding

Entry from home works. However, participants didn't select from suggested amount templates — they entered manually. Ready templates and autofill were valued but not discovered unprompted.

Task 04 · Share requisites · Finding

Hard to find. Users started from "+" (add account), then searched in card settings. "I immediately went to Additional Actions but forgot where requisites are." Almost never done in real life.

Task 05 · IBAN transfer · Finding

Familiar operation. Users who pay utility suppliers recognized the flow. Those who rarely do IBAN transfers were unsure about "Payment purpose" field — what to write and whether it's mandatory.

Task 06 · Utilities · Finding

Address not found. Participants immediately tapped "add address" but couldn't find their accounts listed. "I saw the address suggestions pull up automatically — very convenient" — but only for known addresses.

08 · Outcomes & Learnings

What the data told us
about the new app

The study revealed a clear pattern: high-frequency tasks (transfer, top-up) performed well — users completed them quickly with high satisfaction. Low-frequency tasks (requisites, IBAN, limits) generated the most friction — not because the UI was bad, but because users had no mental model for these flows.

This distinction matters for design prioritization: improving discoverability and progressive disclosure for rare-but-important features will have more impact than refining already-successful flows.

Frequency
= fluency
Tasks users do regularly (transfers, top-up) were completed fast with high satisfaction. Tasks they rarely do (requisites, IBAN, limits) caused confusion regardless of UI quality
Labels
matter
"Transfer to card" vs "Transfer via IBAN" and "Requisites and QR code" — naming decisions caused the most navigational errors. Users search by mental labels, not by app taxonomy
Autofill
= trust
When the app pre-filled data (phone templates, saved payees), users expressed explicit delight and trust. When they had to enter manually, uncertainty followed — even for simple inputs
